title: Hold the side plates up with one hand and slide the dinner plate out from under them
keywords: hold a load up while drawing out from under
instruction: Hold the three side plates up while you slide the dinner plate out from under them, then put the dinner plate on the counter mat. The side plates stay stacked in the cupboard where they are: do not set them down anywhere else, and do not drop them.
context: Taking a plate out of a kitchen cupboard is an everyday act: on an average day in 2024, 63.1% of Americans aged 15 and over prepared food or cleaned up (BLS American Time Use Survey). Side plates are often stacked on the dinner plates, which home organizers call a common nuisance ("You should never have to lift a salad plate to get to a dinner plate"). In a full cupboard there is nowhere to put the small plates down: the floor beside them holds the bowls, and the strip on the other side is narrower than a side plate. Taking them out to the counter first means two extra trips with loose glass through the cupboard opening. So people lift the small stack a few centimetres with one hand and slide the big plate out with the other. Here one arm must hold three loose glass plates up and level while the other draws the plate out from under them: not two separate pick-and-place moves.
setup: All sizes are real. World frame for the tape marks: the counter's front edge is x = 0 at the arm bases, x forward, y left. Cabinet: an IKEA METOD wall cabinet frame, white 18 mm particleboard, 60 cm wide, 37 cm deep, 40 cm high (inside 56.4 x 35.4 x 36.4 cm), door removed, standing on the counter with its open front 37 cm in front of the arm bases, centred between the arms, fixed. Dinner plate: Corelle Winter Frost White 10.25 in (26.0 cm across, 1.9 cm tall, 340 g, Vitrelle glass about 3 mm thick; foot ring 16 cm, flat well 19 cm, rim rising 1.3 cm). Side plates: three Corelle Winter Frost White 6.75 in bread-and-butter plates (17.1 cm, 2.2 cm tall, 130 g each; flat well 11 cm, rim rising 1.6 cm), stacked on the dinner plate's well, 6 mm apart. Bowls: two Corelle Winter Frost White 18 oz cereal bowls (15.9 cm across, 5.1 cm tall, 180 g each), one nested in the other. Counter mat: a 28 x 28 cm, 2 mm silicone dish mat on the counter in front of the cabinet. Layout (setup image): the dinner plate's centre 21 cm in from the cabinet's front edge and 6.5 cm to one side of the cabinet's middle; the bowls on the other side, their rim 2 to 3 cm from the dinner plate's rim, against the inside wall. Only a 7 to 11 cm strip of floor is free on the far side: too narrow for a side plate, and there is no room in front of or behind the plates. Each trial moves the layout (seeded): the bowls stand left or right of the dinner plate (the plates then move 13 cm the other way); the dinner plate's centre +-1 cm in depth and +-2 cm sideways; the side-plate stack up to 1 cm off the dinner plate's centre in any direction; the bowls +-2 cm in depth; the mat's centre +-3 cm each way around a point 20 cm in front of the arm bases, midway between them. Both arms start at the ready pose with the grippers open.
scoring: Score 0 if at any time a side plate's centre moves more than 5 cm (horizontally) from where it started, comes more than 2.5 cm from the side plate under it, tips more than 15 degrees, or drops (falls 1.3 cm or more: in simulation, its centre moves down faster than 0.5 m/s, or 12 mm within 0.1 s). So setting the side plates down anywhere else (the bowls, the counter), carrying them out, letting them ride on the dinner plate or dropping them all score 0. Score 0 also if the dinner plate never comes fully out from under them (its centre never 23.5 cm from the side plates' start centre). Otherwise: 0.35 for drawing the dinner plate out from under them; +0.25 if, at the end, the dinner plate lies flat (tilted under 5 degrees) on the counter (foot within 1 cm of it), its centre within 6 cm of the mat's centre, never dropped, and no gripper within 3 cm of it; +0.25 if the three side plates are back on the cabinet floor (bottom plate's foot within 5 mm of it), each within 4 cm of where it started and within 1.5 cm of the one below, each flat (under 5 degrees), no gripper within 3 cm of them; +0.15 if each bowl moved less than 1 cm, stands upright (under 5 degrees) and the top bowl is still nested (centres within 1 cm). Real trial: tape marks round each plate and bowl at the start, a ruler, a front photo for tilt, and the video for drops and for where the side plates were held.
reset_notes: Put the plates and bowls back on their tape marks from the setup image. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: Real sizes and masses from the maker's pages. Each plate and bowl is one rigid glass body: a foot (a solid disc), a flat well and 14 to 20 flat facets forming the sloped rim, so finger gaps under the rims are real. Stacked plates stand foot on well (6 mm apart; real ones nest a little tighter). Glass friction 0.45. The cabinet is fixed. The mat is drawn only; the plate rests on the counter through it.
scores: Dream-1 run, seed 0: 0.0 (1,200 steps). Scripted demo, reads object poses from the simulator: 1.0 on seeds 0, 1 and 2 (971 to 972 steps). Wrong outcomes: fixed plan 0.0; nobody holds the side plates 0.0; side plates dropped 0.0; dinner plate left in the cupboard 0.75.
